title: A Systematic Comparison of Statistic and Machine Learning Models for Mapping Landslide Susceptibility: Evidence from the 2018 Hiroshima Rainfall-Induced Landslides
content: Landslide Susceptibility Mapping (LSM) is crucial for hazard assessment and land-use planning in landslide-prone regions. This study systematically compares three statistical models—Frequency Ratio (FR), Weights of Evidence (WoE), and Logistic Regression (LR)—with six machine-learning algorithms: Support Vector Machine (SVM), Random Forest (RF), XGBoost, Artificial Neural Network (ANN), k-Nearest Neighbor (KNN), and Decision Tree (DT), to assess landslide susceptibility in Hiroshima Prefecture, Japan. A balanced dataset was generated via stratified sampling of the 2018 inventory of rainfall-induced landslides, incorporating five conditioning factors: slope angle, profile curvature, aspect, elevation, and lithology. Models were evaluated using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score. Among the statistical models, WoE achieved the highest performance (AUC = 0.787; accuracy = 71.3%; F1-score = 0.745), while SVM was the most effective machine-learning model (AUC = 0.802; accuracy = 73.0%; F1-score = 0.743). Both WoE and SVM consistently identified lithology and slope angle as the most influential factors in landslide susceptibility. Field validation confirmed that the WoE susceptibility map accurately identified high-risk areas (recall = 0.77). These findings suggest that although machine-learning models offer only marginal predictive improvements in predictive performance over statistical approaches, WoE provides enhanced interpretability, making it valuable for operational landslide hazard assessment and susceptibility-informed early warning systems.
